title: KMP String Matching
tagline: Find a pattern in O(n+m) by never re-examining text — the prefix function does the bookkeeping.

intuition.analogy: When matching a pattern fails partway, naive search throws away everything and slides the pattern one step. KMP is smarter: it remembers that the part already matched contains repeats, so it can slide the pattern several steps and resume mid-pattern — like remembering you've already memorised a phrase's beginning.
paragraphs: Naive substring search re-checks characters after every mismatch, giving O(n·m). KMP achieves O(n+m) by precomputing how much of the pattern's prefix is also a suffix at each position — the 'failure' or lps (longest prefix-suffix) array.

On a mismatch at pattern position j, instead of restarting, KMP jumps j back to lps[j−1]: the longest prefix that's still matched by the recent text. The text pointer never moves backward, which is the key to linear time.
The lps array is itself built by matching the pattern against itself. Once you have it, matching is a tight loop that powers grep, DNA search, and many string-periodicity problems.
intuition.keyIdea: Precompute the longest prefix-that-is-also-suffix; on mismatch, slide the pattern there instead of restarting.

steps.title: Build lps[]
steps.detail: lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix. Computed by matching the pattern with itself.

steps.title: Scan the text
steps.detail: Advance i (text) and j (pattern) on matches. On a mismatch with j > 0, set j = lps[j−1] (slide); with j == 0, advance i.

steps.title: Report matches
steps.detail: When j reaches m, a full match ends at i−1. Set j = lps[j−1] to continue finding overlapping matches.

complexity.timeReason: Building lps is O(m); scanning the text is O(n) since the text pointer never retreats.
complexity.spaceReason: The lps array for the pattern.

pitfalls: Building lps incorrectly (the 'else len = lps[len−1]' fallback) is the classic bug.
lps stores PROPER prefixes (excluding the whole string).
For all matches (not just the first), reset j = lps[m−1] after each hit.

dryRun.clickMoment: lps[3]=2 means after matching 'ABAB' then failing on the next char, KMP already knows the trailing 'AB' is a valid prefix — so it resumes from pattern index 2 instead of 0, skipping redundant comparisons.

problems.title: Repeated String Match
problems.statement: Fewest repeats of A so that B is a substring.
problems.hint: KMP search of B in repeated A.

approach: If b is a substring of a repeated k times, k is at least ceil(len(b)/len(a)); one extra copy covers an offset overflow.
Repeat a until its length >= len(b), test with KMP/find, then try one more repeat. If still absent, return -1.

problems.title: Shortest Palindrome
problems.statement: Prepend characters to make the shortest palindrome.
problems.hint: lps of s + '#' + reverse(s) gives the longest palindromic prefix.

approach: We prepend the fewest characters to make s a palindrome — equivalent to finding the longest palindromic prefix of s.

Build the string s + '#' + reverse(s) and compute its KMP failure value; that value is the longest prefix of s that is also a suffix of reverse(s) — i.e. the longest palindromic prefix. Prepend the rest reversed.

problems.title: Longest Happy Prefix
problems.statement: Longest non-trivial prefix that is also a suffix.

approach: The longest happy prefix is the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix — exactly lps[n-1] from KMP.
Compute the failure array of the whole string; the answer is the prefix of that length.

problems.title: Find All Anagrams (compare with KMP)
problems.hint: Sliding window of counts (contrast with exact KMP matching).

approach: An anagram is a fixed-length window whose character counts match p's. Slide a window of length |p| over s maintaining a frequency array.
Track how many of the 26 counts match; record a start index whenever all match. (KMP doesn't apply here — anagram matching is a counting window, included to contrast pattern-matching tools.)
